questions.grading:
- Must first count the strings by scanning to the NULL sentinel; `sizeof(strings)/sizeof(strings[0])` does **not** work on a parameter (it is a `char **`), so it loses the counting mark. A fixed-size buffer (e.g. `malloc(100)`) violates "no assumptions about how many strings" (lose a mark).
- Allocate n + 1 bytes and write the `'\0'` terminator at `result[n]`; missing either loses a mark.
- `strings[i][0]` (or `*strings[i]`) is the first character. The paper doesn't say what to do with an empty string `""`; copying its `'\0'` would end the result early, but the question doesn't test this, so don't penalise it.
- Parameter may be written `char *strings[]` or `char **strings`. With no strings (just NULL) the result should be the empty string. Returning a local array is wrong (not on the heap). NULL check on malloc optional.

rubric.item: Correct signature: char *firstChars(char *strings[]) (or char **)
Counts the strings by looping until the NULL element (no sizeof trick, no fixed limit)
Allocates n + 1 chars on the heap
Copies strings[i][0] into result[i] for each string
Null-terminates the result and returns it

questions.grading:
- Count strings by scanning to NULL (no `sizeof` on the parameter, no fixed limit). Allocating n + 1 is enough even though empty strings are skipped; allocating exactly the number of non-empty strings + 1 (two passes) is also fine.
- Last character is `strings[i][strlen(strings[i]) - 1]`. For `""`, `strlen - 1` underflows (size_t) and reads out of bounds, so the empty-string check is essential.
- Needs a separate output index (`k`) because skipped strings leave no gap; using `result[i]` leaves garbage/holes (lose a mark).
- Must null-terminate at `result[k]`. Returning a local array is wrong.

questions.prompt:
**Question 6 (5 points): C I/O and structs**

Here is the definition of a `struct` type. You may assume it's included in your program; you don't have to write it in your answer book.

```c
typedef struct {
  char firstChar;
  char lastChar;
} initials;
```

Write a function that will read the first five lines of a file and record the first and last characters of these lines. By the last character in the line I mean the last character before the end of line character (`'\n'`). It's OK to assume that every line except the last one in the file ends with a `'\n'`, but the last line in the file might not.

The function should take two parameters:
1. The name of the input file (a string)
2. An array of five structs of type `initials`.

Put the first and last characters of the first line into `initials[0]`, the first and last characters of the second line into `initials[1]`, and so on.

Your program must abort the program with an informative error message if any of the following things happen:
- The file does not exist or you don't have read permission for it
- The file contains less than 5 lines
- A line in the file has less than 2 characters (not counting the end-of-line character)

You don't have to worry about any other sorts of I/O errors.

You may assume that no line in the file is more than 50 characters long and that all of the necessary C libraries for I/O have been included in your program.

Here is a header for your function:
```c
void firstAndLast(char *filename, initials structArray[]);
```
questions.grading:
- Buffer size: lines are at most 50 characters, so the buffer needs 50 + 1 (`'
'`) + 1 (`'\0'`) = 52. `char line[51]` would split a 50-char line (the `'
'` would be read as a separate "line"); `char line[50]` is worse. A generous buffer (e.g. 100 or 256) is fine.
- The last line might not end in `'
'`, so the `'
'` must be removed (or the last char found) **only if present**. Blindly using `line[strlen(line) - 2]` as the last char gets the 5th line wrong when it has no newline (lose a mark).
- "Fewer than 5 lines" is detected by `fgets` returning NULL before 5 lines are read. A file of exactly 5 lines whose last line lacks `'
'` is valid.
- Length check is on the line without its `'
'`: `len < 2` aborts (so a blank line or a 1-char line aborts).
- "Abort the program": `exit(EXIT_FAILURE)` / `exit(1)` with a message (stderr preferred, `perror` for fopen). Returning silently from the function does not abort the program. `abort()` is also acceptable.
- Character-by-character reading with `fgetc` is an accepted alternative if it handles the same cases. Lines beyond the fifth are ignored.

rubric.item: Opens the file and aborts with an informative message if fopen fails
Reads 5 lines (fgets with a big enough buffer, or fgetc) and aborts with a message if fewer than 5 lines
Handles the '\n' correctly: strips/ignores it when present, works when the last line has none
Aborts with a message if a line has fewer than 2 characters (excluding '\n')
Stores line[0] and the last character into structArray[i].firstChar / .lastChar for i = 0..4

questions.prompt:
Here is the definition of a `struct` type. You may assume it's included in your program.

```c
typedef struct {
  char firstChar;
  int length;
} lineInfo;
```

Write a function that will read the first **four** lines of a file and record, for each line, its first character and its length (the number of characters before the end-of-line character `'\n'`). It's OK to assume that every line except the last one in the file ends with a `'\n'`, but the last line in the file might not.

The function takes two parameters:
1. The name of the input file (a string)
2. An array of four structs of type `lineInfo`.

Put the information for the first line into `info[0]`, the second line into `info[1]`, and so on.

Your function must abort the program with an informative error message if any of the following things happen:
- The file does not exist or you don't have read permission for it
- The file contains fewer than 4 lines
- One of the first four lines is empty (0 characters, not counting the end-of-line character)

You don't have to worry about any other sorts of I/O errors. You may assume that no line in the file is more than 80 characters long and that the necessary C libraries have been included.

Here is a header for your function:
```c
void firstAndLength(const char *filename, lineInfo info[]);
```

Example: for a file containing the lines `abc`, `d`, `efgh`, `ij` (the last with no `'\n'`), the array ends up holding `{'a',3}`, `{'d',1}`, `{'e',4}`, `{'i',2}`.
questions.grading:
- Buffer must hold 80 chars + `'\n'` + `'\0'` = 82 (larger is fine; 80 or 81 splits a maximum-length line).
- Length must exclude the `'\n'` **only when present**: `strlen(line) - 1` unconditionally is wrong for a final line with no newline (in the example, `ij` would get length 1). Lose a mark.
- Fewer than 4 lines: `fgets` returns NULL early. Empty line: length 0 after stripping (a lone `"\n"`).
- Abort = `exit(EXIT_FAILURE)`/`exit(1)` with a message; just `return` is not enough. Character-by-character `fgetc` solutions accepted.

rubric.item: Opens the file and aborts with an informative message if fopen fails
Reads 4 lines with a big enough buffer and aborts with a message if fewer than 4
Computes the length without the '\n', correct whether or not the last line has one
Aborts with a message if a line is empty
Stores the first character and length into info[i] for i = 0..3
